scenes.dialogue: Your client is accused of murder. He denies it. Does the F I R lead straight to punishment? No. Evidence must be presented, tested and considered.
scenes.shown: Your client is accused of murder. He denies it. Does the FIR lead straight to punishment? No. Evidence must be presented, tested and considered.

scenes.dialogue: Call him Arjun. Follow his contested Sessions trial under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, or B N S S.
scenes.shown: Call him Arjun. Follow his contested Sessions trial under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, or BNSS.

scenes.dialogue: Investigation or trial? Keep them separate. Police investigate, and submit their report under Section One Ninety Three.
scenes.shown: Investigation or trial? Keep them separate. Police investigate, and submit their report under Section 193.

scenes.dialogue: Under Section Two Ten, the Magistrate decides whether to take cognizance of the offence.
scenes.shown: Under Section 210, the Magistrate decides whether to take cognizance of the offence.

scenes.dialogue: Section Two Thirty requires the papers to be supplied free, within fourteen days from the accused's production or appearance. Check both dates carefully.
scenes.shown: Section 230 requires the papers to be supplied free, within 14 days from the accused's production or appearance. Check both dates carefully.

scenes.dialogue: Is the offence triable exclusively by the Court of Session? Then the case is committed there, under Section Two Thirty Two.
scenes.shown: Is the offence triable exclusively by the Court of Session? Then the case is committed there, under Section 232.

scenes.dialogue: The Public Prosecutor then opens the case under Section Two Forty Nine, explaining the accusation and the evidence.
scenes.shown: The Public Prosecutor then opens the case under Section 249, explaining the accusation and the evidence.

scenes.dialogue: Can your client be discharged? Under Section Two Fifty, the application may be made within sixty days from commitment.
scenes.shown: Can your client be discharged? Under Section 250, the application may be made within 60 days from commitment.

scenes.dialogue: Insufficient ground for proceeding? Then the Judge must discharge the accused, and record reasons.
Otherwise, Section Two Fifty One requires a written charge within sixty days from the first hearing on charge. That second clock has a different trigger.
scenes.shown: Otherwise, Section 251 requires a written charge within 60 days from the first hearing on charge. That second clock has a different trigger.

scenes.dialogue: The charge is read and explained, and the plea is recorded. A guilty plea may lead to conviction under Section Two Fifty Two. Arjun contests the charge.
scenes.shown: The charge is read and explained, and the plea is recorded. A guilty plea may lead to conviction under Section 252. Arjun contests the charge.

scenes.dialogue: The prosecution must prove its case. Sections Two Fifty Three and Two Fifty Four govern its evidence: witnesses testify, and documents are presented.
scenes.shown: The prosecution must prove its case. Sections 253 and 254 govern its evidence: witnesses testify, and documents are presented.

scenes.dialogue: Arjun's case: an eyewitness describes the incident, a doctor explains medical findings, and recordings may be produced.
Your turn: cross examine. Could the witness really see clearly? Does the medical evidence actually support the account?
scenes.shown: Your turn: cross-examine. Could the witness really see clearly? Does the medical evidence actually support the account?

scenes.dialogue: And never forget this: an allegation in a charge sheet is not itself proof of guilt.
What about delay? Section Three Forty Six generally requires day to day hearings while attending witnesses remain to be examined.
scenes.shown: What about delay? Section 346 generally requires day-to-day hearings while attending witnesses remain to be examined.

scenes.dialogue: Prosecution witnesses over? Before the defence stage comes a crucial safeguard, under Section Three Fifty One.
scenes.shown: Prosecution witnesses over? Before the defence stage comes a crucial safeguard, under Section 351.

scenes.dialogue: It requires the court to put the circumstances appearing against the accused to him, for his explanation.
A witness places Arjun at the scene? He must get a fair opportunity to answer. This is not cross examination on oath. It is his chance to explain.
scenes.shown: A witness places Arjun at the scene? He must get a fair opportunity to answer. This is not cross-examination on oath. It is his chance to explain.

scenes.dialogue: Every incriminating circumstance must be put to him specifically. The Supreme Court treats this safeguard as no formality. So check the record.
Is there any evidence that he did it? Section Two Fifty Five is the checkpoint. No evidence that the accused committed the offence? The Judge must acquit.
scenes.shown: Is there any evidence that he did it? Section 255 is the checkpoint. No evidence that the accused committed the offence? The Judge must acquit.

scenes.dialogue: Otherwise, Section Two Fifty Six allows defence evidence. Arjun might call a workplace witness, or produce attendance records.
scenes.shown: Otherwise, Section 256 allows defence evidence. Arjun might call a workplace witness, or produce attendance records.

scenes.dialogue: Arjun need not enter the witness box; Section Three Fifty Three lets him testify only on his own written request. Proving guilt remains the prosecution's burden.
scenes.shown: Arjun need not enter the witness box; Section 353 lets him testify only on his own written request. Proving guilt remains the prosecution's burden.

scenes.dialogue: Evidence done? Section Two Fifty Seven provides for final arguments. The prosecutor sums up, and the defence replies.
scenes.shown: Evidence done? Section 257 provides for final arguments. The prosecutor sums up, and the defence replies.

scenes.dialogue: The prosecution links the evidence to the offence. The defence points out weaknesses, inconsistencies or reasonable doubt.
Tie every argument to the record, because a lawyer's argument is not, by itself, proof of a disputed fact.
Arguments are over. How long can the judgment take? Under Section Two Fifty Eight, the Sessions Judge must deliver it within thirty days of the arguments ending.
scenes.shown: Arguments are over. How long can the judgment take? Under Section 258, the Sessions Judge must deliver it within 30 days of the arguments ending.

scenes.dialogue: That period can be extended to forty five days, but only with written reasons. Note the exact date the arguments end.
scenes.shown: That period can be extended to 45 days, but only with written reasons. Note the exact date the arguments end.

scenes.dialogue: The court decides whether Arjun's guilt has been proved beyond reasonable doubt, and gives reasons for acquittal or conviction.
Common mistake: these thirty or forty five days start after arguments. They set no deadline for the whole case from the F I R.
scenes.shown: Common mistake: these 30 or 45 days start after arguments. They set no deadline for the whole case from the FIR.

scenes.dialogue: If Arjun is convicted, Section Two Fifty Eight, sub section Two, requires a hearing on sentence before punishment.
scenes.shown: If Arjun is convicted, Section 258(2) requires a hearing on sentence before punishment.

scenes.dialogue: Come prepared. The court considers the sentencing material and the parties' submissions, then passes the lawful sentence. Any appeal is a separate process.
Magistrate trial? The provisions change. Warrant cases on a police report follow Sections Two Sixty One to Two Sixty Six.
scenes.shown: Magistrate trial? The provisions change. Warrant cases on a police report follow Sections 261 to 266.

scenes.dialogue: Complaint warrant cases follow Sections Two Sixty Seven to Two Seventy, with evidence taken before the charge.
scenes.shown: Complaint warrant cases follow Sections 267 to 270, with evidence taken before the charge.

scenes.dialogue: Both conclude under Sections Two Seventy One to Two Seventy Three. Summons cases follow Sections Two Seventy Four to Two Seventy Eight, with no formal charge.
scenes.shown: Both conclude under Sections 271 to 273. Summons cases follow Sections 274 to 278, with no formal charge.

scenes.dialogue: Remember the main Sessions route: charge and plea, prosecution evidence, the accused's explanation, any defence evidence, arguments and judgment.
And sentencing follows only if there is a conviction. Always check the case type, and each deadline's exact starting point.
